# Lesson plan — PHP for Dynamic Web Pages

**Course:** Computer Science and ICT · **Title:** Programming · **Lesson:** PHP for Dynamic Web Pages
**Place in the curriculum:** ICT expansion — Egypt (2026-11-14) — in the title Programming on the ICT course ladder (TITLES.md). Built new from Egypt's student books (Egypt Ministry of Education and Technical Education / Ministry of Education), because no existing lesson in the course covers this thing as its own lesson.
**The one thing this lesson teaches:** A page generated by a program on the server in response to this request.
**This lesson's own level:** It stands on the earlier lessons of its title and on the book's own order — it follows the book's lessons in sequence, so its neighbours in the book are its natural companions. It stands alone for a learner landing on it directly.

A lesson plan also says **what goes on top of the lesson**: at the exact places marked below, the lesson page carries an add-on — an image, a GIF, a video, an audio. Every slot is written as **"a picture of …" in words, plus one little line saying what the student does with it**. The words carry the picture while the course is built and while the AI learns from the books; on the website the real add-on is dropped into that slot and the little explanation stays as the student's guide. GIFs come first where a thing must be shown moving — a GIF here is 1–2 seconds.

## Sub lessons
The parts of this lesson, in order — the list the learner sees from the start, locked ahead, each opening when the one before it is proved:

1. **Dynamic pages — generated when asked** — A **static** page is a finished file: every visitor gets the same bytes. A **dynamic** page is **generated**: a program on the server builds the page's HTML **in response to this request** — reading the database, choosing what this visitor asked for — and sends the result. **PHP** is the language the book uses for that generating program: PHP code sits inside the page file, runs **on the server** (the visitor never sees it — only its output), and its whole job is producing the page, often out of database content. The dictionary becomes dynamic the moment its term pages are PHP: add a term to the database, and the site shows it — no page edited by hand.
2. **The PHP page at work — request, database, answer** — The working rhythm is the project's heartbeat: the browser **requests** a PHP page, perhaps with a choice attached (which term? which letter?); the server runs the PHP, which **queries MySQL**; the answers come back as data; the PHP **builds HTML around the data** and the server sends that HTML to the browser. Every part of the Grade 11 project meets here — the Expression Web pages provide the pattern the data is poured into, the MySQL database created earlier provides the content, and the Add_Term page is this same rhythm running in reverse, storing instead of showing. Egypt teaches PHP inside one real site because a dynamic page only makes sense attached to data someone actually wants.

Gate pool: all questions of the sub lesson — no hardness ranking is written in questions/, so the sub lesson's whole question set is the gate pool.

## Before this lesson
- Recommended first: the earlier lessons in Programming on the ladder. Recommended, never forced — a learner may land on this lesson directly, and it stands alone.
- Egypt's own way is kept: see the placement and own-way notes in lesson/sources.md.

## What the learner can do when it ends
1. A page generated by a program on the server in response to this request.
2. The same finished file — the same bytes.
3. Request, query the database, build HTML around the data, send it.
4. A choice — which term, which letter.

## What you need
Paper and a pencil, and a computer with the program this lesson uses, if available.

## The run of the lesson (in order)
1. **Do it first** — In Egypt's Grade 11 project, the dictionary site's pages must stop being fixed text: a term page should show what is in the database now, not what was typed into HTML last month. PHP is the book's answer — pages generated by a program, on the server, at the moment they are asked for. (lesson/lesson.md).
2. **The explanation** — the lesson text in lesson/lesson.md, in its parts in order.
   - ADD IMAGE: a picture of dynamic pages — generated when asked as the lesson describes it — the student studies the picture and names what each part shows.
   - ADD GIF: a GIF of the php page at work — request, database, answer in action — the student watches once, then says what changed and why.
   - ADD AUDIO: a voice reading the lesson's key names and definitions aloud, in the order the lesson gives them — the student listens once through, then reads the same lines aloud along with the voice. (Audio is a described slot in this build; no audio file is made.)
3. **Say it to your companion** — the companion block in lesson/lesson.md.
   - ADD VIDEO: the script in video-script.md, filmed — the lesson in the super-simple voice (made later, when videos are made).
4. **Questions** — from questions/: multiple-choice, true-false, matching, short-answer — served at the learner's level and teaching-mix (levels.md).
5. **Hands-on** — hands-on.md.
6. **Do It Yourself** — the doing block at the end of lesson/lesson.md.

## If the learner is stuck
Returns to the one thing this lesson teaches and works it with a smaller example of their own, then tries the stuck part again. Mixes this lesson's tools or terms with a neighbouring lesson's → place the two side by side and name the difference in one sentence each.
